title: Reading and Interpreting Real-life Graphs
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Algebra
summary: Read and interpret real-life graphs with several sections or two lines — journeys, costs, filling containers — explain their shape and say what an intersection means.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Read and interpret real-life graphs that have more than one part — for example a journey made of several stages, or two lines drawn on the same axes. Explain why a graph has its shape (steep, flat, straight or curved) and what it means when two graphs cross (intersect). [8As.07]

blocks.text: Graphs are used everywhere to show how one quantity changes with another: distance with time, cost with distance, the depth of water with time. In Stage 8 the graphs have **more than one component** — several straight sections joined together, or two lines on the same grid. You must be able to read values accurately, explain what each part of the graph shows in the real situation, and say what is happening where two lines cross.
1. Key words

items: axis (plural axes)
محور — the horizontal and vertical number lines of a graph
scale
مقياس الرسم — what each square on an axis is worth
component / section
جزء — one part (one straight piece) of a graph
distance–time graph
منحنى المسافة والزمن — shows how far something is from a place as time passes
steep / steeper
شديد الانحدار — rising or falling quickly
horizontal
أفقي — flat: the quantity is not changing
rate
معدل — how fast something changes, e.g. km per hour, litres per minute
speed
السرعة — distance ÷ time
intersection
نقطة التقاطع — the point where two graphs cross
fixed charge
رسوم ثابتة — an amount you pay before anything else

blocks.text: 2. Read the graph before you answer

items: Read the **title** and the **labels on both axes**, including the units (minutes or hours? km or m? $?).
Work out the **scale**: what one small square is worth on each axis. For example, if 5 small squares cover 10 km, one small square is 2 km.
Look at each **section** of the graph separately: is it going up, going down, or flat? Is it steep or gentle? Straight or curved?
Look for **intersections** — places where two graphs cross.
When you read a value, use a ruler: go across or up from the axis to the line, then to the other axis. Give the units.

rows: The quantity increases at a steady (constant) rate.
A faster rate (e.g. a higher speed or a higher price per unit).
No change — on a distance–time graph, the person has stopped.
The quantity decreases at a steady rate — e.g. coming back towards the start.
The rate of change is increasing (speeding up / filling faster).
The rate of change is decreasing (slowing down / filling more slowly).
At that moment both quantities are equal: same place at the same time, or same cost.

blocks.text: 3. Distance–time graphs with several sections
On a distance–time graph, time goes across and distance from a fixed place goes up. The **steepness** shows the speed: speed = distance ÷ time for that section.

4. Two graphs on the same axes — what an intersection means

items: Why straight lines? Each extra kilometre always costs the same amount, so the cost rises at a constant rate.
Why does P start at $12? That is the fixed charge you pay even for 0 km. Q starts at $0 (the origin).
Why is Q steeper? Q charges more for each km ($5 instead of $3).
The lines cross at (6 km, $30): for a 6 km journey both companies cost $30.
Shorter than 6 km → Q's line is lower, so Q is cheaper. Longer than 6 km → P is cheaper.

items: **X (straight sides):** every centimetre of height needs the same amount of water, so the depth rises steadily — a **straight line**.

**Y (wide at the bottom):** at first the water spreads over a wide area, so the depth rises slowly. As the container gets narrower, the same amount of water makes the depth rise faster — the graph **gets steeper**.

A container with straight sides that suddenly changes width (e.g. a wide box with a narrow tube on top) gives two straight sections, the second steeper.

blocks.title: ازاي تقرا الرسم البياني
items: الأول اقرا عنوان كل محور والوحدات، واحسب كل مربع صغير يساوي كام.
الخط الأفقي (المستوي) يعني مفيش تغيير — في رسم المسافة والزمن يعني الشخص واقف.
كل ما الخط يبقى أشد انحدارًا، يبقى المعدل أسرع (سرعة أعلى أو سعر أعلى لكل وحدة).
نقطة تقاطع الخطين معناها إن القيمتين متساويتين في اللحظة دي: نفس المكان في نفس الوقت، أو نفس التكلفة.

blocks.text: 6. Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — Use the graph of Yasmin's ride in section 3. (a) How far from home was Yasmin after 30 minutes? [1] (b) How long did she stop for altogether? [1] (c) In which section was she cycling fastest? Explain how you know. [1] (d) Work out her speed on the way home in km/h. [2]

rows: Go up from 30 on the time axis to the line, then across: **6 km**. (Section A rises 8 km in 40 min, i.e. 2 km every 10 min.)
Flat sections: 40–60 min and 90–110 min. 20 + 20 = **40 minutes**.
**Section E** — it is the steepest line (12 km in 40 minutes).
12 km in 40 minutes. 40 min = 40/60 h = 2/3 h. Speed = 12 ÷ 2/3 = 12 × 3/2 = **18 km/h**. (Or: 12 km in 40 min → 3 km in 10 min → 18 km in 60 min.)

blocks.text: Common mistake: reading the speed as 12 ÷ 40 = 0.3 and calling it km/h. That is km per **minute**; change the time to hours first.

**Worked example 2** — Use the graph of Ahmed and Karim in section 4. (a) At what time do Ahmed and Karim meet, and how far are they from Town A? [2] (b) How far apart are they at 09:30? [1] (c) Explain why Karim's graph slopes downwards. [1]

rows: The lines cross at **10:00**, **4 km** from Town A.
At 09:30 Ahmed is 2 km from A and Karim is 10 km from A: 10 − 2 = **8 km apart**.
The graph shows distance from Town A. Karim is travelling towards Town A, so his distance from A is getting smaller.

blocks.text: Common mistake: thinking that a line going down means "going downhill". On a distance–time graph it means moving back towards the starting place.

**Worked example 3** — Use the taxi graph in section 4. (a) Find the cost of an 8 km journey with each company. [2] (b) Mona travels 4 km. Which company is cheaper, and by how much? [2] (c) What does the point where the lines cross tell you? [1]

rows: At 6 km both companies charge the same amount, $30. Below 6 km Q is cheaper; above 6 km P is cheaper.

rows: The tank fills from 0 to 40 litres: 40 ÷ 4 = **10 litres per minute**.
Flat: the amount stays at 40 litres for 2 minutes (the tap is off and the tank is not emptying).
The tank empties from 40 litres to 0 in 8 minutes: 40 ÷ 8 = **5 litres per minute**. This line is less steep, so it empties more slowly than it filled.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Water is poured at a steady rate into container Z (narrow at the bottom, wide at the top) from section 5. Sara says: "The graph of depth against time is a straight line because the water is poured at a steady rate." Is she correct? Explain. [1]

**Answer:** No. The water flows in at a steady rate, but the container gets wider, so each litre raises the depth by less and less. The depth rises quickly at first and then more slowly, so the graph is a curve that gets less steep. A straight line would only happen if the sides were straight up (the same width all the way).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Not checking the scale: one small square may be 2 km, 5 litres or 20 metres — not 1.
Mixing minutes and hours when working out speed in km/h.
Thinking a flat section means "moving at a steady speed". On a distance–time graph, flat means **stopped**.
Thinking a line going down means going downhill. It means the quantity (e.g. distance from home) is decreasing.
Reading the wrong line when two graphs are drawn — use the key and follow the colour or label.
Describing an intersection as "where the lines meet" without saying what it means in the situation (same place and time, same cost…).
Forgetting units in the answer (km, minutes, $, litres).

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Use the graph to find …" — show your reading lines on the graph and write the value with units.
"Write down the time when …" or "How long did … stop?" — look for flat sections and read both ends.
"Explain why the graph is steeper / curved / flat in this part" — link the shape to the situation (faster, slower, stopped, container wider).
"What is the significance of the point where the graphs intersect?" — say both quantities are equal there, in context, with the values.
"Which company is cheaper for … ? Give a reason." — compare the heights of the lines at that value.
"Match each container to its graph" or "Sketch the graph" — straight sides give straight lines; wider gives less steep; narrower gives steeper.

questions.ms: 1 mark: Company A has a fixed charge (booking fee) of $40 that you pay even before any days are added / at 0 days. Do not accept "because it is more expensive".
questions.e: Company A charges a fixed fee of $40 (paid however many days you hire) plus $20 per day. Company B has no fixed fee, so its line starts at 0.

questions.q: Water is poured at a steady rate into a bowl that is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top. Which describes the graph of depth against time?
c: A curve that gets less steep
questions.e: At the narrow bottom the depth rises quickly; as the bowl gets wider the same amount of water raises the depth less, so the graph gets less steep.

questions.q: Two cups of tea cool down. On a graph of temperature against time, their curves cross at (6 minutes, 45 °C). What does this tell you?
c: After 6 minutes both cups are at 45 °C
Both cups cool at the same rate for 6 minutes
Each cup takes 45 minutes to cool by 6 °C
questions.e: An intersection means the two quantities are equal at that moment: 6 minutes after the start, both cups have the same temperature, 45 °C. It does not tell you that their rates are the same.

questions.q: Hassan walks from his home to a shop at a steady speed for 10 minutes. The shop is 800 m away. He stays in the shop for 5 minutes, then runs home in 4 minutes. Sketch a distance–time graph of his trip, with distance from home on the vertical axis.
questions.ms: 1 mark: straight line from (0, 0) to (10, 800). 1 mark: horizontal line at 800 m from 10 to 15 minutes. 1 mark: straight line from (15, 800) down to (19, 0), steeper than the first section. Axes labelled with units (time in minutes, distance in m).
questions.e: Section 1: a straight line from (0 min, 0 m) up to (10 min, 800 m). Section 2: a flat line at 800 m from 10 to 15 min (in the shop). Section 3: a straight line down from (15, 800) to (19, 0). It is steeper than the first section because running is faster (800 m in 4 min instead of 10 min).

blocks.title: Remember
items: Check the axis labels, units and scale before reading any value.
Steeper = faster rate; flat = no change (stopped); sloping down = decreasing (e.g. returning).
Speed = distance ÷ time — change minutes to hours for km/h.
Where two graphs intersect, both quantities are equal: say what that means in the story, with the values.
Containers filled at a steady rate: straight sides → straight line; getting wider → less steep; getting narrower → steeper.
